questions.question: Define a transaction and distinguish between cash and credit transactions. Why must every transaction be supported by a source document?
questions.expected_answer: A transaction is an event that changes the financial position of a business and can be measured in money. A cash transaction is paid at the time it takes place (notes and coins, card or EFT); a credit transaction is supplied now and paid later. Source documents prove the transaction took place, give the details needed to record it (date, amount, parties, purpose), allow checking and protect against errors and fraud, and must be kept (for SARS, five years).

questions.question: Describe four services a bank provides to a business. A salon's bank balance was R8 000; it received R14 600 and paid rent R6 000, wages R5 400 and products R1 200. Calculate the closing balance.
questions.expected_answer: Services: keeping money safe in a current account; receiving payments (deposits, card machines, incoming EFTs); making payments (EFTs, debit orders, cards); overdrafts and loans; monthly bank statements. Payments = 6 000 + 5 400 + 1 200 = R12 600. Closing balance = 8 000 + 14 600 − 12 600 = R10 000.

questions.question: Explain the purpose of subsidiary journals. Name the two cash journals, what each records and two source documents for each, and give three reasons for using separate journals.
questions.expected_answer: Subsidiary journals are books of first entry in which transactions of one type are recorded in date order from source documents before being posted to the ledger. CRJ: all money received — duplicate receipts, cash register roll, bank statement/EFT notifications. CPJ: all money paid out — EFT payment confirmations, cash slips or invoices, bank statement (debit orders, bank charges), formerly cheque counterfoils. Reasons: efficiency (columns are totalled and posted once a month), division of work between clerks, control (easy to check every document is recorded and to find errors).
